claims.text: A hybrid CALPHAD and machine-learning framework using elemental melting temperatures and bulk moduli can accurately predict melting temperature and entropy of fusion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The combinatorial growth of binary interactions causes standard CALPHAD to underestimate solid-solution stability in high-component-count alloys.
The target domain comprises equimolar 4- to 6-component alloys selected from refractory and transition-metal elements.
Experimental melting data for these alloys is sparse or unreliable at temperatures above 2000 °C.
Mean elemental melting temperature and mean bulk modulus can be combined with CALPHAD phase calculations and a configurational-entropy filter to estimate melting temperature and entropy of fusion.
Requiring the fraction of fully assessed binary systems, fAB, to equal 1 provides a thermodynamically credible screening domain.
The model is applied to alloys containing between 3 and 6 elements.
Maximum use temperature can be estimated as 0.8 times the melting temperature.
Configurational entropy rises in proportion to ln(N).
The number of binary interactions in an N-component alloy scales as N(N-1)/2.
The rapidly increasing number of binary interactions drives intermetallic formation as the number of components increases.
Bulk modulus and melting temperature act as proxies for the strength of the interactions governing phase stability.
The formation enthalpy of intermetallic compounds is essential for phase-stability prediction but is difficult to estimate because no general model is available.
Difficulty estimating intermetallic formation enthalpies causes CALPHAD to overestimate intermetallic stability and underestimate solid-solution stability.
Machine learning can capture the net thermodynamic effect of a high-component-count alloy without explicitly modeling every binary interaction.
The hybrid model will predict melting temperature and entropy of fusion with less than 5% error relative to experiments.
The hybrid model will correctly identify solid-solution stability where standard CALPHAD predicts intermetallic formation.
Pandat v.8.1 has been used for CALPHAD phase-diagram calculations of equimolar multi-principal-element alloy systems.
Standard CALPHAD predicts that the solid-solution fraction at the melting temperature falls from 30% for N=3 to 5% for N=6.
The mean-property approximation may fail for non-equiatomic or strongly segregated alloys.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the method bypasses the need for exhaustive assessment of binary interactions, but the stated validity domain requires fAB=1, meaning every binary subsystem in each screened alloy must already be fully assessed.
